answer.label: Not Napoleon Bonaparte — an ancient proverb
answer.authorDates: Chabrias, Athenian general, died 357 BC · recorded by Plutarch, c. 46–120 AD
answer.sourceLine: This is a floating classical proverb, not a Napoleon original. Plutarch’s ‘Moralia’ credits the Athenian general Chabrias with the idea that an army of deer led by a lion is more to be feared than an army of lions led by a deer. Per Quote Investigator ↗, Napoleon did employ the saying (recorded in an 1823 St Helena memoir) but he explicitly credited “the Athenian general,” and the ‘sheep’ wording seen today first surfaced in 1736 with no connection to him.

source.excerpt: That an army of deer commanded by a lion is better than an army of lions commanded by a deer.
trail: Earliest documented form: Plutarch’s ‘Moralia’ credits the Athenian general Chabrias, per Quote Investigator ↗.
The animal has drifted over centuries — stags/deer, then ‘sheep’ from 1736, then donkeys/asses in the 1800s — per Quote Investigator ↗.
Wikiquote ↗ files the ‘sheep’ version under “Misattributed,” tracing the printed Napoleon credit only to Tarle’s ‘Napoleon’ (1941).
War History Online ↗ lists it among “famous things Napoleon never said.”
source.excerptNote: Napoleon’s own phrasing as recorded in the 1823 ‘Memoirs…Dictated by the Emperor at Saint Helena’ — note the ‘deer’ wording and the credit to an unnamed Athenian general, not the modern ‘sheep’ version.

source.rightsNote: The saying is an ancient proverb documented in pre-1931 public-domain sources — Plutarch’s ‘Moralia,’ a 1736 English text carrying the ‘sheep’ wording, and the 1823 St Helena memoir with the ‘better than’ form. No single modern author owns the phrasing; it is a floating proverb long in the public domain.

author.heading: The Athenian general behind the proverb
author.metaLine: died 357 BC · Athenian general · saying preserved by Plutarch (c. 46–120 AD)
author.bio: Chabrias was a prominent Athenian general of the 4th century BC, active in campaigns across the Aegean and in Egypt. The Greek biographer Plutarch, writing centuries later in the ‘Moralia,’ records Chabrias’s maxim that an army of deer led by a lion is more to be feared than an army of lions led by a deer — the ancient seed of the line now misattributed to Napoleon.

misattribution.heading: A proverb pinned on everyone
misattribution.intro: This is one of history’s most-travelled proverbs, pinned in turn on nearly every famous commander. The through-line is that almost no one who gets the credit actually originated it.

items.why: Napoleon ↗ did use the saying — the 1823 St Helena memoir records him invoking it — but he credited “the Athenian general,” not himself, and used ‘deer,’ not ‘sheep.’ Wikiquote ↗ files the sheep version under “Misattributed.”

Widely shared as Alexander’s (“I am not afraid of an army of lions led by a sheep…”), but Wikiquote ↗ lists it only as an ancient proverb loosely attributed to Alexander among many commanders, with no primary source placing it in his mouth.

items.who: Philip of Macedon, Julius Caesar, Iphicrates
items.why: The same saying was reassigned to Philip (1563), Julius Caesar (1655), and Iphicrates (1673) as it circulated — a hallmark of a floating proverb, per Quote Investigator ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The earliest documented form credits the Athenian general Chabrias in Plutarch’s ‘Moralia’; the ‘sheep’ wording only appears from 1736, per Quote Investigator ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The saying flatters a comforting idea about leadership: that a bold leader multiplies the courage of ordinary followers, while a timid leader squanders even the fiercest. That universality is exactly why it has been reassigned across two millennia to whichever great commander a writer had in mind.

Its migration is also a case study in how wording drifts. Plutarch’s Chabrias spoke of deer; by 1736 the animal had become sheep; the 19th century preferred donkeys. Napoleon, who genuinely used the maxim, was careful to credit “the Athenian general” — a modesty the internet has quietly erased.
detailsBody: The version now attributed to Napoleon in print traces only to Yevgeny Tarle’s biography ‘Napoleon’ (1941), long after Napoleon’s death, which is why Wikiquote treats it as misattributed rather than sourced.
context.pull: Napoleon used the line — and credited someone else for it.
